AD.title: A mountain valley held in common
AD.body: In the Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a system of shared land ownership dates to the thirteenth century. Stone paths and summer settlements trace how people worked the high pastures.

AE.title: Circular tombs from the Bronze Age
AE.body: At Al Ain, people built circular stone tombs around 2500 BCE. The surrounding desert also preserves wells and earthen buildings left by communities that settled there long ago.

AF.title: A line of blue above a valley
AF.body: High in a river valley in Ghur, twelfth-century builders raised the Minaret of Jam to 65 metres. Near the top, a band of blue tile breaks up the patterns worked into the brick.

AG.title: A board game on a turtle’s back
AG.body: In 2015, Antigua and Barbuda gave Queen Elizabeth II a wooden turtle made for the game of warri. Its back is a board with hollows for 48 stone counters.

AL.title: A castle full of churches
AL.body: Much of Berat’s hilltop castle dates to the thirteenth century. Inside its walls stand Byzantine churches as well as mosques built under Ottoman rule.

AM.title: A monastery inside the mountain
AM.body: Medieval builders at Geghard carved most of the monastery’s churches and tombs directly into the rock. The complex stands at the entrance to the Azat Valley.

AO.title: Stories drawn in sand
AO.body: In eastern Angola, Lunda Cokwe artists and their neighbours have passed stories down through drawings called sona. An artist dots a patch of damp sand with two fingers, then draws lines around the dots.

AR.title: Hands still on the wall
AR.body: Thousands of years ago, people stencilled the outlines of their hands on rock at Cueva de las Manos. Among the handprints are paintings of guanacos, relatives of llamas that still live in the region.

AT.title: A railway climbs the mountains
AT.body: Between 1848 and 1854, builders laid the Semmering Railway across 41 kilometres of mountain terrain. They used both tunnels through the mountains and tall bridges over the valleys.

AU.title: What sits under the shells?
AU.body: Sydney’s Opera House opened in 1973. Its three groups of interlocking roof shells shelter two main performance halls and a restaurant.

AZ.title: A plateau full of pictures
AZ.body: At Gobustan, people carved pictures into boulders across a plateau. Researchers have counted more than 6,000 engravings in a rock-art tradition that stretches back thousands of years.

BA.title: A bridge rebuilt over the Neretva
BA.body: Mostar grew up around a bridge over the Neretva River. After the Old Bridge was destroyed in the 1990s, the city rebuilt the crossing that had linked its two banks.

BB.title: A town of winding streets
BB.body: Bridgetown grew between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. While many colonial towns in the Caribbean were laid out in grids, its streets followed a winding pattern.

BD.title: Paintings that travel by rickshaw
BD.body: In Dhaka’s rickshaw workshops, painters have handed their craft down through families. They turn three-wheelers into moving galleries, painting everything from birds to film stars.

BE.title: An elevator for boats
BE.body: Engineers fitted the Canal du Centre with hydraulic lifts to carry boats between water levels. Four lifts from the era of nineteenth-century industrial canals still stand along one short stretch.

BF.title: Women who decorate a royal court
BF.body: At Tiébélé, the Kasena royal court grew from the sixteenth century onward. Women have passed down the meanings of the designs they paint on its earthen buildings.

BG.title: A rider on a cliff
BG.body: Near Madara, a carved horseman rides across a cliff face. Inscriptions beside him recount events between 705 and 801, turning the rock into a record of early Bulgarian history.

BH.title: Where the pearl boats set out
BH.body: Pearl divers once sailed from the southern tip of Muharraq Island to offshore oyster beds. In the city, their trade left its mark in shops, storehouses and the homes of pearl merchants.

BI.title: Drums arranged around a drum
BI.body: Burundi’s royal drumming tradition brings poetry, dance and music together. Drummers place an odd number of drums in a semicircle around a central drum that sets the beat.

BJ.title: Eleven kings shared one enclosure
BJ.body: From 1625 to 1900, twelve kings ruled Abomey in succession. All but one built their palaces inside the same enclosure of earthen walls.

BN.title: Streets above a river
BN.body: For centuries, people at Kampong Ayer have built their homes on stilts over the Brunei River. Wooden walkways and bridges connect the settlement.

BO.title: A hill carved into a gathering place
BO.body: Above the old town at Samaipata stands a huge carved rock. Archaeologists think the hill served as a ceremonial centre between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries.

BR.title: A capital drawn like a bird
BR.body: In the 1950s, planner Lúcio Costa and architect Oscar Niemeyer helped build Brasília from the ground up. Seen from above, the layout of its districts has often been compared to a bird in flight.

BS.title: From paper to parade
BS.body: In the early 1800s, enslaved Africans in the Bahamas used holiday time to recreate festivals from home. In the Junkanoo tradition they passed on, makers now turn cardboard and crepe paper into towering parade costumes.

BT.title: Sixteen masks at Drametse
BT.body: In the village of Drametse, dancers have honoured a Buddhist teacher with a masked drum dance. Sixteen dancers take part, moving slowly for peaceful deities and quickly for wrathful ones.

BW.title: Thousands of paintings in the Kalahari
BW.body: At Tsodilo in the Kalahari Desert, artists left more than 4,500 rock paintings in an area of just ten square kilometres. Local communities also revere the hills as a place of worship.

BY.title: Paper lace for the stage
BY.body: In Belarus, cut-paper art called vytsinanka once decorated church interiors and icons. Artists later found places for it on postcards and theatre sets, cutting intricate patterns with scissors or even a chisel.

BZ.title: Christmas moved from door to door
BZ.body: In the Christmas Bram of Gales Point Manatee, villagers have carried an African-rooted tradition from home to home. Drummers accompany singers who trade lines back and forth along the way.

CA.title: Norse houses in Newfoundland
CA.body: At L’Anse aux Meadows, archaeologists found traces of houses built by Norse settlers in the eleventh century. The wooden frames and turf walls resemble buildings in Greenland and Iceland.

CD.title: The dance behind Congolese rumba
CD.body: In the two Congos, musicians trace Congolese rumba to an older dance called nkumba, meaning “waist” in Kikongo. Women helped shape both its love songs and its religious music.

CF.title: Four voices, room to improvise
CF.body: Aka communities in the southwest have passed down songs built from four interlocking vocal parts. A singer can vary a line in the middle of a performance while the others carry on.

CG.title: A capital that moved
CG.body: In the Téké kingdom, the capital of Mbé moved to a new site each time a king died. Sacred forests grew where the old capitals had stood.
CG.sourceName: Congolese Ministry of Culture and Arts · UNESCO

CH.title: A building plan drawn on parchment
CH.body: The abbey library at St Gall preserves an early architectural plan drawn on parchment. It sits among the manuscripts collected by a monastery whose history goes back to the eighth century.

CI.title: From cassava to tiny grains
CI.body: Lagoon communities in Côte d’Ivoire have handed down a way of turning cassava roots into attiéké. Cooks mix ground cassava with fermented cassava, then steam the little grains.

CL.title: The stone figures of Rapa Nui
CL.body: Between the tenth and sixteenth centuries, people on Rapa Nui built shrines and raised enormous stone figures called moai. The island’s sculptors belonged to a society of Polynesian origin.

CM.title: Walls put together without mortar
CM.body: In Cameroon’s Mandara Mountains, sixteen archaeological sites preserve dry-stone buildings known as Diy-Gid-Biy. Their builders likely worked between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries.

CN.title: An army made of clay
CN.body: In 1974, a buried army of terracotta figures came to light at the tomb of China’s first Qin emperor. The clay warriors have individual features, and the ensemble includes horses and chariots.

CO.title: A street becomes a picture gallery
CO.body: Families in Galeras have passed down a way of staging pictures with their own bodies. On an evening called “dressing the streets,” performers hold still to recreate scenes from stories and daily life.

CR.title: Stone spheres beneath the soil
CR.body: In the Diquís Delta, people shaped stone spheres more than two metres across. Layers of sediment hid some for centuries, preserving them where their makers had placed them.

CU.title: A song that leads the dance
CU.body: In Cuban son, generations of musicians brought African and European influences together. A singer can improvise verses as dancers follow the pulse of the bass.

CV.title: Songs of leaving and coming home
CV.body: Cape Verde’s morna tradition brings music together with poetry. Singers have improvised verses about parting, reunion and the ocean, often to a guitar accompaniment.

CY.title: A duel fought in rhymes
CY.body: At Greek Cypriot weddings and fairs, poet-singers have challenged each other to make up rhyming couplets on the spot. A violin or lute often accompanies this contest called tsiattista.

CZ.title: Glass beads for the Christmas tree
CZ.body: Families in northern Bohemia have blown glass beads since the late 1700s. For Christmas ornaments, makers cut the beads apart and thread them onto wire to build different shapes.

DE.title: An instrument built for its room
DE.body: For centuries, German organ makers have worked with musicians to design each instrument for the space where it will be played. The room itself helps determine the organ they build.

DJ.title: A wedding gift with a puzzle
DJ.body: In the Djiboutian wedding tradition of xeedho, a mother prepares a gift of preserved camel meat for her new son-in-law. The carved container is wrapped and tied with carefully hidden ropes.

DK.title: Two stones, a change of faith
DK.body: At Jelling, one carved stone recalls old Nordic beliefs. Another stands beside a church and records Denmark’s turn toward Christianity in the tenth century.

DM.title: A canoe from one tree
DM.body: Dominica’s Kalinago canoe builders hollowed out a single gommier tree trunk with fire and stone tools. They widened the hull and fitted wooden ribs to hold its shape.

DO.title: Before it was a dance, it was a party
DO.body: In the Dominican Republic, the word bachata once referred to a lively get-together. The music that took its name blends bolero with sounds from other Caribbean traditions.

DZ.title: A desert drawn by its witnesses
DZ.body: At Tassili n’Ajjer, people drew and carved animals and scenes of daily life on the rock. The pictures reach back to around 6000 BCE and record how life on the edge of the Sahara changed.

EC.title: A hat worth months of weaving
EC.body: Coastal Ecuadorian communities have passed down the craft of weaving hats from toquilla palm fibres. A simple hat can take a day, while the finest can take up to eight months.

EE.title: A boat from one tree
EE.body: In Soomaa, boatbuilders have taught apprentices to turn a single tree, usually an aspen, into a canoe. After hollowing the trunk, they spread its sides to widen the boat.

EG.title: A rescue on the Nile
EG.body: Between 1960 and 1980, an international rescue campaign saved ancient monuments in Nubia from rising water. The temples of Ramses II at Abu Simbel were among them.

ER.title: Cinemas in the highlands
ER.body: In the 1930s, builders in Asmara applied modern Italian designs to cinemas, hotels and places of worship. The highland city also preserves neighbourhoods that grew outside colonial planners’ designs.

ES.title: Water once crossed above the street
ES.body: Roman builders carried water into Segovia on an aqueduct with two layers of arches. A long stretch still rises above the old city.

ET.title: A city where emperors returned
ET.body: Aksum’s political power waned in the tenth century, but Ethiopian emperors continued to come there to be crowned. The old city still has great stone pillars cut from single blocks.

FI.title: Fiddle tunes learned by ear
FI.body: For more than 250 years, fiddlers in Kaustinen have passed down a style of playing by ear. The area’s repertoire runs to hundreds of tunes, many meant for dancing.

FJ.title: The capital before Suva
FJ.body: In the early 1800s, merchants built wharves and warehouses around existing villages at Levuka. The seaside town later served as Fiji’s first colonial capital.

FM.title: A city of handmade islands
FM.body: Off Pohnpei, builders at Nan Madol created more than a hundred small islands using basalt and coral. Between 1200 and 1500, they built stone homes, palaces and temples across them.

FR.title: A metal roof made room upstairs
FR.body: Nineteenth-century builders in Paris covered many roofs with zinc. It was light enough to need a smaller frame, leaving people more space to live in the attic.

GA.title: Iron in a forest clearing
GA.body: At Lopé-Okanda, archaeologists have found traces of ironworking alongside old settlements in caves and on hilltops. These remains trace the paths of different groups through Gabon’s forest and savanna.

GB.title: A gorge gave iron a new job
GB.body: At Ironbridge Gorge in England, engineers used iron to build a bridge during the eighteenth-century Industrial Revolution. The crossing helped change how later engineers thought about bridge building.

GD.title: A boat gets godparents
GD.body: Shipwrights on Carriacou and Petite Martinique have built wooden boats for centuries. At a traditional launch, young godparents reveal the name embroidered on a red flag.

GE.title: Homes shaped like towers
GE.body: In Upper Svaneti, families lived in stone tower-houses that also served as places of defence. The mountain village of Chazhashi preserves this medieval building tradition.

GH.title: A proverb you can wear
GH.body: Ghanaian weavers have passed down the craft of making kente on horizontal looms. Finished cloths can take their names from proverbs or situations in everyday life.

GM.title: Circles beside a river
GM.body: Over more than 1,500 years, communities along the River Gambia raised stone pillars in circles beside burial mounds. The remains of this shared landscape extend into Senegal.

GN.title: A wooden instrument that remembers an epic
GN.body: In Nyagassola, a family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a sacred xylophone with twenty wooden slats. Its music has carried epic stories of the Mali Empire across generations.

GQ.title: A necklace you could spend
GQ.body: On Bioko island, Bubi women wore necklaces made of shells that also served as money. One large necklace could be worth twelve gallons of palm oil.

GR.title: Monasteries on stone pillars
GR.body: Monks began settling the steep sandstone peaks of Meteora in the eleventh century. By the time fresco painters decorated the monasteries in the 1500s, whole communities lived high above the valley.

GT.title: Giant kites for the ancestors
GT.body: Around the turn of the twentieth century, giant kite-making took root in Santiago Sacatepéquez and Sumpango. Families spend months building the frames and decorating the faces with coloured tissue paper.

GW.title: An ox at a coming-of-age ceremony
GW.body: On the Bijagós Islands, Bijagó initiates have worn a mask called dungn’be that represents a domesticated ox. A wood-and-horn example entered the Royal Museum for Central Africa in 1974.

GY.title: Gothic arches made of wood
GY.body: Builders in Georgetown gave St George’s Cathedral the pointed arches and soaring windows of a Gothic church. Between 1889 and 1894 they built it almost entirely in timber, right down to the walls above its low masonry foundations.

HN.title: Three chapters in a Maya city
HN.body: At Copán, a Maya city, archaeologists can trace three stages of building in its public squares and citadel. People had left the city by the early tenth century.

HR.title: Seventy-one faces in stone
HR.body: Builders of the cathedral in Šibenik carved 71 faces of men, women and children into a band of stone. Work on the cathedral stretched from 1431 to 1535.

HT.title: A soup to celebrate freedom
HT.body: In colonial Haiti, pumpkin soup was reserved for enslavers. After independence, Haitians made joumou soup a celebration of freedom, cooking it with vegetables, meat, plantains, pasta and spices.

HU.title: A village keeps an older rhythm
HU.body: Much of Hollókő grew in the 1600s and 1700s. People deliberately preserved the village, leaving a picture of rural life before twentieth-century farming transformed the countryside.

ID.title: Buddhas hidden in plain sight
ID.body: At Borobudur in Java, builders set 72 openwork shrines around the temple’s circular terraces, each enclosing a Buddha statue. The temple dates to the eighth and ninth centuries.

IE.title: A harp carved from willow
IE.body: Harpists in Ireland have played for more than a thousand years. Some earlier harps were carved from one piece of willow and had metal strings plucked with the fingernails.

IL.title: A desert road scented with incense
IL.body: From the third century BCE to the second century CE, traders carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. Four Nabataean towns in the Negev served the route.

IN.title: A memorial you descend into
IN.body: In eleventh-century Gujarat, builders made Rani-ki-Vav, a stepwell, as a memorial to a king. Visitors went down toward the water through levels of carved stone.

IQ.title: A ring hidden in a fist
IQ.body: In the Iraqi game of al-muhaibis, one team hides a ring in a player’s hand. Traditionally played during Ramadan, it challenges the other side to work out who has it.

IR.title: Water travelling underground
IR.body: In dry parts of Iran, people dug tunnels called qanats to carry groundwater to farms and homes. A gentle slope let gravity move the water for kilometres.

IS.title: Making laws under the open sky
IS.body: In 930, Icelanders set up an outdoor assembly at Þingvellir. For two weeks each year, people gathered there to make laws and settle disputes.

IT.title: A city spread across little islands
IT.body: Venice began in the fifth century and grew across 118 little islands in a lagoon. By the tenth century it had become a major power at sea.

JM.title: The sounds that became reggae
JM.body: Musicians in western Kingston drew on earlier Jamaican music and on soul and rhythm and blues from North America. Out of ska and then rocksteady grew reggae.

JO.title: A city built into its own cliffs
JO.body: Petra stood where caravan routes from Arabia, Egypt and Syria met. Its Nabataean builders constructed parts of the city and carved others straight into the surrounding rock.

JP.title: Silk behind the thatched roofs
JP.body: In the mountain villages of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama, families raised silkworms and grew mulberry trees. Their large farmhouses are easy to recognize by their steep thatched roofs.

KE.title: A town made of coral stone
KE.body: Builders in Lamu used coral stone and mangrove wood to shape homes with verandas, courtyards and carved doors. Since the nineteenth century the Swahili town has also hosted major Muslim festivals.

KG.title: A sacred mountain above the Silk Roads
KG.body: For more than 1,500 years, travellers have used the peaks of Sulaiman-Too as a landmark near Osh. People carved animals, human figures and geometric shapes into its rock.

KH.title: Several capitals in one park
KH.body: Angkor preserves more than a single temple. Between the ninth and fifteenth centuries, the Khmer Empire built a succession of capitals there, including the city of Angkor Thom.

KI.title: Stones to steer by
KI.body: On Arorae, researchers documented eight stones set out in different directions. They may have helped canoe navigators learn where stars appeared on the horizon before a voyage to another island.

KM.title: Towns shaped by the Indian Ocean
KM.body: Six old towns in the Comoros grew from settlements dating to at least the eleventh century. Trade and migration across the Indian Ocean helped shape their streets and buildings.

KN.title: The train that followed the sugar harvest
KN.body: When Saint Kitts finished its narrow-gauge railway in 1926, the trains ran seasonally to bring freshly cut sugar cane to a factory near Basseterre. In 2003, the line began carrying sightseers.

KP.title: Paintings inside a kingdom’s tombs
KP.body: Artists of the Koguryo kingdom painted the inside walls of some tombs. Only a small fraction of the thousands of Koguryo tombs found across Korea and China contain these murals.

KR.title: A library carved in wood
KR.body: Between 1237 and 1248, craftspeople carved Buddhist texts onto about 80,000 wooden printing blocks. At Haeinsa Temple, fifteenth-century buildings still shelter the collection.

KW.title: Weaving made its way to school
KW.body: In 2018, Kuwait’s Al Sadu Society started a programme to teach teachers a traditional weaving craft. School textile exhibitions at Sadu House gave students a place to show what they made.

KZ.title: A puppet powered by a musician’s fingers
KZ.body: In the Kazakh tradition of orteke, strings connect a wooden mountain goat to a musician’s fingers. As the player plucks a two-stringed dombyra, the little goat dances and taps a drum.

LA.title: A plateau of stone jars
LA.body: Iron Age communities in what is now central Laos carved enormous stone jars for funerary rites. More than 2,100 of them gave the Plain of Jars its name.

LB.title: A city that helped letters travel
LB.body: Byblos was already inhabited in the Stone Age. It later became a Phoenician city linked to the spread of the Phoenician alphabet around the Mediterranean.

LC.title: Two flowers with their own choirs
LC.body: By 1844, writers were already describing two rival flower societies in Saint Lucia, the Rose and the Marguerite. Each still has its own songs and annual feast.

LI.title: A postage stamp made of stitches
LI.body: Liechtenstein began issuing its own postage stamps in 1912. In 2019 it celebrated the country’s 300th anniversary with a stamp made using embroidery.

LK.title: A stairway through a lion
LK.body: In the fifth century, King Kassapa built a capital on the steep rock of Sigiriya. A giant brick-and-plaster lion once framed the stairs leading up toward the summit.

LR.title: A new way to write Vai
LR.body: In the early 1800s, people in what is now Liberia began writing the Vai language in a script of their own. Its invention went on to inspire writers of neighboring languages, including Mende and Kpelle.

LS.title: Stories painted under rock shelters
LS.body: In the Maloti-Drakensberg mountains shared by Lesotho and South Africa, San artists painted beneath natural rock shelters. The paintings preserve traces of the spiritual life of communities that lived there for millennia.

LT.title: A hanging garden made from rye
LT.body: Lithuanian families have woven geometric ornaments called sodai from grain stalks, often rye. They hung these straw “gardens” above a cradle to wish a baby happiness.

LU.title: A procession that hops
LU.body: A procession at Echternach appears in records as early as 1100. Each year participants mark a feast honouring Saint Willibrord by hopping through the medieval town.

LV.title: A trading city built outward
LV.body: Riga prospered on trade with central and eastern Europe in the Middle Ages. In the 1800s the city expanded beyond its old centre, first with wooden buildings and then with flowing Art Nouveau designs.

LY.title: An upstairs route through town
LY.body: In the oasis town of Ghadamès, families traditionally stored supplies on the ground floor. Women used open rooftop terraces while covered passages linked the streets below.

MA.title: The woman remembered in Fez
MA.body: Tradition credits Fatima al-Fihri with founding the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in the ninth century. People came to pray there, and the mosque grew into a center of learning.

MC.title: A museum with ship names on its walls
MC.body: Look up at Monaco’s Oceanographic Museum and you can find the names of twenty scientific ships carved high on the building. Prince Albert I chose the ships himself.

MD.title: Measuring Earth across borders
MD.body: In the 1800s, surveyors working in what is now Moldova helped measure a line reaching from Norway to the Black Sea. Their chain of measurements helped establish the shape of the Earth.

ME.title: A harbour where artists trained
ME.body: In the Middle Ages, merchants came to Kotor’s sheltered Adriatic harbour to trade. The town also had schools where craftspeople learned stonework and the art of painting religious icons.

MG.title: The children went on tour too
MG.body: In Madagascar’s central highlands, families have passed down hiragasy, a performance that mixes speeches, dancing and songs. Children learned by travelling with their parents and joining their performances.

MH.title: A map to study before sailing
MH.body: Marshallese navigators made stick charts to teach how ocean swells bend around islands. A learner studied the pattern before setting out to sea.

MK.title: A dancer keeps the circle balanced
MK.body: In the village of Dramche, dancers have linked up in a semicircle for kopachkata at weddings and holidays. The middle dancer balances the two sides as they move to the drums.

ML.title: Timbuktu was a place to study
ML.body: In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, students gathered at Sankore and other Islamic schools in Timbuktu. Alongside the desert trade, scholarship helped make the city famous.

MM.title: Cities with moats and waterworks
MM.body: The Pyu kingdoms built walled cities on the dry plains of the Irrawaddy basin between about 200 BCE and 900 CE. Some parts of their irrigation systems have stayed in use.

MN.title: Deer carved into standing stones
MN.body: Between about 1200 and 600 BCE, people in central Mongolia carved stags into tall standing stones. Some rise four metres above the ground near Bronze Age burial mounds.

MR.title: Towns built for the caravans
MR.body: In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, people founded towns such as Chinguetti to serve caravans crossing the Sahara. Homes with patios crowded along narrow streets around a mosque.

MT.title: A chamber beneath the limestone
MT.body: Around 2500 BCE, builders carved the vast underground complex of Ħal Saflieni. People used the space to bury their dead, though it may have started as a sanctuary.

MU.title: An island beat passed down
MU.body: On Rodrigues, an island of Mauritius, enslaved communities created a form of music and dance called sega tambour. A drum leads the rhythm, with other players striking a triangle and clapping percussion instruments.

MV.title: Carpenters who worked in coral
MV.body: Early Maldivian mosque builders carved blocks of coral stone and fitted them together. Their craft drew on island boatbuilding techniques, and some walls still carry elaborate carved designs.

MW.title: Rock painting into the twentieth century
MW.body: At Chongoni, Chewa farmers kept painting on rock well into the 1900s. The same hills also preserve paintings by BaTwa hunter-gatherers who lived there from the late Stone Age.

MX.title: Maya stories carved into walls
MX.body: Palenque flourished between 500 and 700 CE. Its Maya artists carved scenes from their mythology in shallow relief on the city’s buildings.

MY.title: A rainforest record inside a cave
MY.body: Borneo’s Niah caves preserve evidence of people living with the rainforest for at least 50,000 years. Archaeologists have found rock paintings and even burials shaped like boats.

MZ.title: An orchestra made of xylophones
MZ.body: Chopi musicians in southern Mozambique have played in orchestras of up to thirty wooden xylophones. Beneath each wooden key, a gourd sealed with beeswax helps give the instrument its sound.

NA.title: Footprints carved in stone
NA.body: At Twyfelfontein, hunter-gatherers carved rock pictures of animals and of the tracks people and animals leave behind. The site preserves a record of their practices across at least 2,000 years.

NE.title: Streets follow old campsites
NE.body: When Tuareg groups settled in Agadez in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, they kept the boundaries of their former camps. The street plan of the old city still follows those lines.

NG.title: Fields on the slopes, a palace above
NG.body: At Sukur, people cut terraces into the slopes below their chief’s hilltop palace. Ironworking once flourished there, and remains of that industry are still part of the village landscape.

NI.title: A character who talks back to power
NI.body: In the satirical play El Güegüense, an Indigenous character faces off with Spanish colonial officials. The earliest scripts probably date to the early 1700s, and performers in Diriamba still stage it with music and dance.

NL.title: Windmills put to work on water
NL.body: At Kinderdijk, people began draining land for farming and settlement in the Middle Ages. Windmills, reservoirs and dykes became parts of one system for managing the water.

NO.title: Houses built for ducks
NO.body: On Norway’s Vega islands, fishing families gathered the soft down of eider ducks. They even built small shelters where the birds could nest.

NP.title: Three cities, three great squares
NP.body: The Kathmandu Valley preserves historic Durbar Squares in Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. Together with the valley’s Hindu temples and Buddhist stupas, they record generations of Nepali building and craft.

NR.title: Twelve points on a star
NR.body: When Nauru became independent in 1968, it raised a flag with a twelve-pointed white star. Each point represents one of the island’s twelve traditional tribes.

NZ.title: Protecting sacred summits
NZ.body: In 1887, Ngāti Tūwharetoa sought protection for the sacred peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. Those mountain summits became the heart of Tongariro National Park.

OM.title: Sharing water by gravity
OM.body: In Oman, farming communities built channels called aflaj to carry spring water and groundwater to fields. Gravity moved the water, and villages developed rules for sharing it.

PA.title: Neighbours build a house together
PA.body: In parts of Panama, families have learned to build quincha houses at community “mud meetings.” Neighbours stamp and mix clay, then work it into walls, often with music and a shared meal.

PE.title: A city carved into the Andes
PE.body: Inca builders fitted the terraces, ramps and stone walls of Machu Picchu into a mountain ridge. This city in the forest stands more than 2,400 metres above sea level.

PG.title: Swamps became gardens
PG.body: At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people reclaimed swampy ground for growing plants. Archaeologists have found evidence of cultivation there stretching back around 7,000 years.

PH.title: From pineapple leaves to cloth
PH.body: In Aklan, families have woven fine piña cloth from fibres stripped by hand from pineapple leaves. Weavers traditionally used old coins of different values to weigh the fibres.

PK.title: Town planning thousands of years ago
PK.body: In the third millennium BCE, people laid out the Indus Valley city of Moenjodaro according to a plan. A high, fortified district rose above an orderly lower town.

PL.title: Chapels carved from salt
PL.body: People began mining rock salt at Wieliczka and Bochnia in the thirteenth century. Underground, miners carved statues and entire chapels out of the very material they came to extract.

PS.title: A hillside turned into fields
PS.body: Around Battir, generations of Palestinian farmers built stone terraces into the hills. Some carried water from underground springs to vegetable plots, while other terraces supported vines and olive trees without irrigation.

PT.title: Tiles and iron above the street
PT.body: Portuguese kings lived in Évora in the fifteenth century. In later centuries, residents decorated whitewashed houses with colourful tiles called azulejos and balconies made of wrought iron.

PW.title: Villages on now-empty islands
PW.body: Palau’s Rock Islands look uninhabited today, but old stone village sites tell another story. Stone walls, rock art and burial sites preserve the story of communities who lived here before leaving in the 1600s and 1700s.

PY.title: A polka slowed down
PY.body: Guarania music emerged in Paraguay in the early twentieth century. It drew on Paraguayan polka, pairing a slow, lilting rhythm with words in Guarani.

QA.title: A pearl town preserved by sand
QA.body: Merchants from Kuwait founded Al Zubarah, a coastal town that thrived on pearl diving and trade in the late 1700s. Desert sand later covered its fishermen’s huts and courtyard homes, helping preserve them.

RO.title: How earth became red pottery
RO.body: In Horezu, generations of potters have worked local earth into red clay by washing, kneading and even trampling it. Each potter develops a personal touch for shaping it by hand.

RS.title: A town painted its own story
RS.body: In the 1930s, self-taught artists in Kovačica began painting village life in bright oils. Later generations kept the style and added scenes from their own times.

RU.title: Wooden churches on a lake island
RU.body: Carpenters built two wooden churches on Kizhi, an island in Lake Onega, in the eighteenth century. In 1862, an eight-sided wooden clock tower joined them.

RW.title: Dance training included public speaking
RW.body: Rwanda’s intore dancers traditionally trained at schools called itorero. Along with movement and music, they learned public speaking, games and principles of government.

SA.title: Decorated doorways in the desert
SA.body: At Hegra, Nabataean craftspeople left monumental tombs with carved fronts. The decorated façades date from the first century BCE to the first century CE.

SB.title: A shawl made of money
SB.body: In the 1970s, a maker on the island of Malaita put strings of shell money together to make a bridal shawl. The white, black and red discs formed patterns across the shoulders.

SC.title: A dance around the forest fire
SC.body: Enslaved Africans brought moutya to Seychelles in the eighteenth century and danced it at night in the forest. In the tradition they passed on, musicians warm their drums over a fire before playing.

SD.title: A kingdom beside the Nile
SD.body: The rulers of Kush built a royal city at Meroe near the Nile. Its pyramids and temples are reminders of a kingdom whose rulers also governed Egypt for nearly a century.

SE.title: A Viking trading town on a lake
SE.body: In the ninth and tenth centuries, people lived and traded at Birka on an island in Lake Mälar. Finds there and on neighbouring Adelsö reveal how far the trading networks of Viking-age Europe reached.

SG.title: Rubber research in a city garden
SG.body: Singapore’s Botanic Gardens began in 1859. By 1875 the gardens had become a centre for plant research, including work that helped shape rubber growing across Southeast Asia.

SI.title: Beekeeping made it into poetry
SI.body: Slovenian beekeepers have shared their knowledge in print since the eighteenth century. Alongside practical advice, writers recorded poems and sayings about bees.

SK.title: The wire that mended a pot
SK.body: In the eighteenth century, craftspeople in what is now Slovakia bent and twisted wire by hand to mend cookware. The repair skill grew into drotárstvo, an art used to make sculptures as well as tools.

SL.title: A woven cloth that once served as money
SL.body: In Sierra Leone, weavers made elaborate kpokpo cloth by joining narrow strips so their patterns lined up. A fine cloth was once valuable enough to use as currency.

SM.title: A republic on a mountain
SM.body: The historic centre of San Marino dates to its beginnings as a medieval city-state in the thirteenth century. Its government still works in the old city on Mount Titano.

SN.title: Hills made of shells
SN.body: Over generations, people in the Saloum Delta gathered shellfish and built up great mounds of discarded shells. Some of these human-made hills stretch for hundreds of metres.

SO.title: Cattle painted in a rock shelter
SO.body: Thousands of years ago, artists at Laas Geel painted cattle in several colours on the walls and ceilings of rock shelters. Alongside the animals are people with their arms spread wide.
SO.sourceName: French Ministry of Culture · French Archaeology Abroad

SR.title: Builders blended two ways of working
SR.body: Paramaribo grew as a Dutch colonial town in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Local builders combined Dutch architectural designs with their own materials and techniques, giving the old city its distinctive houses.

SS.title: A stool by day and a pillow by night
SS.body: A Dinka Tuich woodworker turned a single tree branch into a three-legged stool. Collected in 1979, it doubled as a headrest.

ST.title: A trial staged outdoors
ST.body: In São Tomé and Príncipe’s tchiloli theatre tradition, a festival crowd gathers outdoors to watch a trial unfold. About thirty actors play the families, imperial court and officials involved in the case.

SV.title: A farming village sealed in time
SV.body: Around 600 CE, a volcanic eruption buried the farming community of Joya de Cerén. What it covered survived so well that archaeologists can study the everyday lives of the people who worked the land.

SY.title: Broken glass got another life
SY.body: Damascus glassblowers have turned waste glass into lamps, cups and vases. They melt the pieces in a handmade brick oven, then blow the glass into shape through a hollow metal rod.

SZ.title: The glass animals that brought a factory back
SZ.body: When the glassworks at Ngwenya closed, a family who collected its little glass animals went looking for the makers. They helped reopen the factory in 1987.

TD.title: Pictures tucked into desert canyons
TD.body: In the sandstone canyons of Ennedi, people painted and carved thousands of images. Their pictures survive on cave walls and beneath rock shelters in what is now the Sahara.

TG.title: A house shaped like a tower
TG.body: In Koutammakou, which stretches across the border with Benin, Batammariba families have built distinctive tower-houses from earth. A single house is called a takienta.

TH.title: Farming and metalworking at Ban Chiang
TH.body: At Ban Chiang, archaeologists found traces of prehistoric farmers who also made and used metal. The settlement helped show how those two skills developed in Southeast Asia.

TJ.title: Where herders and farmers met
TJ.body: More than 4,000 years ago, Sarazm stood between mountain pastures and a valley suited to farming. Traders connected the settlement with distant places as far away as the Indian Ocean.

TL.title: A cloth for welcoming a baby
TL.body: In Timor-Leste, families have welcomed newborns with handwoven tais. Weavers traditionally used cotton and plant dyes, with colours and patterns that could identify their community.

TM.title: Four thousand years in an oasis
TM.body: At Merv, travellers on the Silk Road could stop at a Central Asian oasis. The ruins there preserve around 4,000 years of settlement in one place.

TN.title: A huge arena in a small town
TN.body: In the third century, Roman builders put up an amphitheatre at El Jem with space for as many as 35,000 spectators. Its great stone arches still stand in the town.

TO.title: Poetry danced in rows
TO.body: Tonga’s lakalaka tradition took shape in the nineteenth century and revived in the twentieth. In big performances, hundreds of people sing, clap and dance together in rows.

TR.title: Towns below the valley floor
TR.body: People in Cappadocia carved homes and sanctuaries directly into the rock. Around Göreme, underground towns preserve traces of a way of living that goes back to the fourth century.

TT.title: How an oil drum learned a tune
TT.body: In the late 1930s, musicians in Trinidad and Tobago made music on buckets, bins and pans. Experimenting with the shape of the metal led to steelpans made from oil drums that could play whole melodies.

TV.title: A wooden box keeps the beat
TV.body: Tuvalu’s fatele tradition brings singing and dancing to weddings and welcomes. Musicians have used a wooden box called a pokisi and an empty tin called a kaapa to keep time.

TZ.title: Chinese porcelain on an African island
TZ.body: Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, merchants at Kilwa traded Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and Arabian dishes. Their island port was part of a trading network across the Indian Ocean.

UA.title: The musicians who had a secret language
UA.body: Ukrainian travelling musicians who played the kobza or wheel lyre formed guilds to protect their rights. Traditionally an apprentice had to learn the performers’ secret language as well as their music.

UG.title: A palace turned royal resting place
UG.body: In 1882, a palace for the king of Buganda was built on Kasubi Hill. Two years later it became a royal burial place, with a great circular building at its heart.

US.title: Villages tucked into cliffs
US.body: In what is now southwestern Colorado, Ancestral Pueblo people built villages on top of the Mesa Verde plateau and homes in the cliffs below. Some of the stone cliff dwellings had more than a hundred rooms.

UY.title: Walls that ripple like fabric
UY.body: When the Church of Atlántida opened in 1960, its brick walls rose in waves supporting a rippling roof. Engineer Eladio Dieste used reinforced brick to give a heavy material those curves.

UZ.title: A Silk Road city of schools
UZ.body: Bukhara has stood on the Silk Road for more than 2,000 years. Along its old streets are a tenth-century tomb and many madrasas, or schools, built in the seventeenth century.

VA.title: The missing wing of St Peter’s Square
VA.body: In the 1600s, Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the curving rows of columns around St Peter’s Square. He was also asked to build a third wing, but the plan ended when Pope Alexander VII died in 1667.

VC.title: Loops across a shelter wall
VC.body: At Buccament on Saint Vincent, earlier islanders engraved rows of spirals, dots and loops across the back of a rock shelter. The rows stretch about eight metres.
VC.sourceName: St Vincent and the Grenadines National Trust

VE.title: Clouds inside a university hall
VE.body: Between 1940 and 1960, architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva designed a university campus in Caracas that brought art into its buildings. Alexander Calder’s sculptural “Clouds” became part of the main auditorium.

VN.title: A trading port kept its street plan
VN.body: Between the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries, Hội An was a busy port. Its buildings and surviving street layout show how local builders and traders from abroad shaped the town together.

VU.title: A story told in a single line
VU.body: Sand artists in Vanuatu have traced complex designs with one finger, following an imagined grid without breaking the line. The same drawings can be made in volcanic ash or clay.

WS.title: A mat woven a millimetre at a time
WS.body: Samoan weavers have made fine ceremonial mats called ‘ie Samoa from strips of pandanus sometimes just a millimetre wide. A single mat can take months or even years to finish.

YE.title: A city that grew upwards
YE.body: In sixteenth-century Shibam, planners fitted a city inside its walls by building upward. The old tower houses still give this Yemeni town its distinctive skyline.

ZA.title: Houses that travel with a herd
ZA.body: In the Richtersveld, Nama herders have moved with their animals as the seasons change. Portable homes built from rush mats let families take their shelter along.

ZM.title: A dance the miners took up
ZM.body: Kalela began in Zambia’s Luapula Province during colonial times and was adopted by mine workers. Dancers sing as they move forward and back in rows to a drumbeat.

ZW.title: A trading city in medieval Africa
ZW.body: Between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, ancestors of the Shona people made Great Zimbabwe an important centre for trade. The city covered nearly eighty hectares.
